Audited Results for the year ended 30 June 2026

Helium One Global (AIM: HE1), the primary helium explorer in Tanzania with a 50% working interest in the Galactica-Pegasus helium development project in Colorado, USA, is pleased to announce the Company’s audited results for the year ended 30 June 2026.
Successfully completed Electrical Submersible Pump ("ESP") testing at ITW-1

Produced over the equivalent of 250,000 barrels ("bbl") of water during a 20-day testing programme, with flow rates of up to an equivalent of 16,400 barrels per day ("bpd") - representing a six-fold increase compared with natural flow rates achieved during the 2024 Extended Well Test ("EWT")
Achieved sustained helium concentrations of 5.4% (air corrected) at surface, with a maximum concentration of 9.2% (air corrected)
Formally awarded a 480 km2 Mining Licence (“ML”) in southern Rukwa in July 2025, representing Tanzania’s first helium mining licence and largest mining licence awarded in the country

The Company, and the Government of Tanzania executed the Framework Agreement and the Shareholders’ Agreement for the joint venture company, Songwe Helium Ltd, in which Helium One Global Ltd holds an 83% interest
Commenced a formal farm-out process in May 2026 to identify and select a suitable industry partner for the southern Rukwa Helium Project and discussions with a number of parties ongoing.
Commissioned the Piñon Canyon processing facility, with six development wells drilled and tied in, and achieved first gas in December 2025
In June 2026, Blue Star Helium (“Blue Star” or the “Operator”) entered into an initial 3-month helium purchase and sales agreement covering all helium produced at the Piñon Canyon Plant
Clive Carver appointed Non-Executive Chairman in April 2026
Appointment of Nishant Dighe as a Non-Executive Director and Sarah Cope as an Executive Director
The Company raised a total of £13.8 million during the year
Total comprehensive loss attributable to the equity holders of the Company of US$3,413,295, a decrease compared with US$4,857,406 for the year ended 30 June 2025
The Group’s net assets as at 30 June 2026 were US$67,919,638, compared with US$53,202,847 at 30 June 2025
At 30 June 2026, the Group’s cash position was US$6,552,494 (30 June 2025: US$3,152,755).
First helium sales achieved in July 2026 in the US
At the end of August, the helium purchase and sales agreement was extended to 31 March 2027
Raised approximately £3 million in October 2026 to cover the expected operating costs for the remainder of the current financial year
The Operator plans to deepen 3 existing wells at Galactica during Q4 2026, followed by a further 9 wells in 2027, subject to permission being granted

Blue Star Helium continues to advance commercial discussions on CO2 co-production and liquefaction, with a focus on expanding gas processing capacity and supporting revenue growth through 2026 and into 2027

At southern Rukwa, the Company is evaluating new development targets for further drilling and testing, with activity likely to focus on primary fractured Basement targets at additional locations across the 480 km2 Mining Licence area
The Company looks forward to the outcome of the formal farm-out process
The Company-owned Epiroc 220 drilling rig remains warm stacked in the southern Rukwa region and operationally ready to support future activity
Helium’s role in high-technology applications continues to underpin its strategic importance, in a market influenced by demand, supply and geopolitical developments
Clive Carver, Chairman of Helium One, commented:
“This has been an incredibly busy period for the Company which has seen us deliver some very significant milestones as well as undertaking some incredibly important initiatives.

Helium One have transitioned from an exploration company into a company with production in the US and a world class development project in Tanzania where the team have proved up the potential of the project and which we are now looking to further progress through bringing in a suitable industry partner.

Helium remains a commodity in demand and we are advancing our projects to be a key player in delivering this in the future.  I would like to take this opportunity to thank all our stakeholders and shareholders for their continued support during the year and going forward in what we believe will be another important year for the Company as we continue to deliver our strategy and build on what we have achieved in the last year.”
“We have made significant progress across both projects, advancing our strategy to become a helium producer with a diversified portfolio.

In the US, we worked with Blue Star to commission the Piñon Canyon facility, achieve first gas and commence helium sales.  In Tanzania, successful ESP testing at southern Rukwa demonstrated the project’s potential. We also secured Tanzania’s first helium mining licence and the country’s largest mining licence, executed a framework agreement with the Tanzanian Government for Songwe Helium Ltd., and launched a formal farm-out process.

These milestones provide a strong foundation for the next phase of development. Our focus remains on progressing both projects and realising their potential to help meet the increasing global demand for helium.

I would also like to take this opportunity to thank our team, partners, local communities, landowners and Government stakeholders for their contribution, and our shareholders for their continued support. I look forward to providing further updates as we advance our projects.”
The Company announces the appointment of Cavendish Capital Markets Ltd (“Cavendish”) as joint broker to enhance investor reach and research coverage.
Cavendish will work alongside, the Company’s Nominated Adviser and existing joint broker, Panmure Liberum Ltd and the Company’s existing joint broker, Axis Capital Markets Ltd.
For further information please visit the Company’s website: www.helium-one.com
Graham Jacobs, Finance and Commercial Director

Helium One Global, the primary helium explorer in Tanzania with a 50% working interest in the Galactica-Pegasus helium development project in Colorado, USA. The Company holds helium licenses within two distinct helium project areas, across two continents and has the potential to become a strategic player in resolving a supply-constrained helium market.

The Company’s flagship southern Rukwa Project is located within the southern Rukwa Rift Basin in south-west Tanzania. This project entering a full appraisal and development stage following the success of the 2023/24 exploration drilling campaign, which proved a helium discovery at Itumbula West-1 and, following an extended well test (“EWT”), successfully flowed 5.5% helium continually to surface in Q3 2024.

Following the success of the EWT, the Company filed a Mining Licence (“ML”) application with the Tanzania Mining Commission in September 2024 and the 480km2 ML was formally awarded to the Company in July 2025.
The Company also owns a 50% working interest in the Galactica-Pegasus helium development project in Las Animas County, Colorado, USA. This project is operated by Blue Star Helium Ltd

and successfully completed a six well development drilling campaign in H1 2025. The completion of the development programme is a key component of the broader Galactica-Pegasus development strategy; aimed at progressing the helium and CO2 discoveries to near-term commercial production.

This programme has seen a systematic approach to developing the extensive Lyons Formation reservoir. The programme has delivered encouraging results, in line with expectations, consistently encountering good helium (up to 3.3% He) and CO2 concentrations in the target formation and demonstrating promising flow potential. The initial Galactica wells were tied into first gas in Q4 2025, with further wells coming onstream in 2026 for both helium and CO2 production.
I am pleased to present the audited financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2026.

I was appointed Non-Executive Chairman in April 2026 and these are my first set of annual results for the Company. As such, the strong progress during the period under review is the result of the team here before me and I give full credit to my predecessor James Smith for all that he and they have achieved.
While the Company has a number of worthy secondary objectives our clear prime mission is to be a sustainable commercial success for the benefit of our shareholders.
In industries where producers do not set the price, returns to shareholders are principally a function of the offtake price and the “producers” production performance.

Helium is no different to any other market where the price is the result of the interaction of demand and supply. The worldwide demand for helium, with its growing applications notably in the electronics/semiconductors, healthcare (MRI), and aerospace industries is, in my opinion, set for continued steady growth.

Helium supply, however, is at best uncertain. For helium to be produced as a by-product of methane or carbon dioxide, as is the case with around 95% of global production, it requires the production of that methane or carbon dioxide to be commercial as no rational producer would suffer losses on methane or carbon dioxide just to produce the associated helium. Producers of helium where methane and carbon dioxide is not the prime activity, such as ourselves, therefore have a distinct advantage.

More important though on world prices is the ongoing disruption to some of the key helium producers caused by the impact of the Iran war and Russian sanctions, which has reduced global supply by an estimated 33% and increased prices by over an estimated 100%.  It has also led to countries such as the United States designating helium as a critical material and others such as China imposing restrictions on the re-export of helium.
In summary, the outlook for helium is both strong now and for the foreseeable future.

None of this helps in attaining the Company’s prime goal of sustained commercial success without the cost-effective production of helium. In July 2026, after the period end, the Company sold its first helium from the Galactica-Pegasus helium development project in Colorado, USA, and continues to do so, moving the Company up the value chain from the ranks of helium explorer to helium producer.
In Tanzania at our Southern Rukwa project a farm-out process is underway in which we are seeking the involvement of an industry heavyweight to move the project forwards at pace.
A detailed account of operational progress is set out in the Chief Executive’s report.

In recent times we have adopted a conservative approach to our public statements and have sought to ensure that communication with our investor base, both by way of company announcements and presentations, and in institutional investor meetings and widely available investor platform updates, has been transparent, clear and equal across all investor groups.

While the approach on the content of our public statements will continue, we recognise we need to do more to keep shareholders updated with news of your Company’s progress and look forward to providing more regular updates across the various channels going forwards.

The Company raised a total of £13,875,000 during the year under review by way of the issue of 3,936,585,438 new ordinary shares. These proceeds were used to advance our southern Rukwa and Galactica-Pegasus projects.

In October 2026 we also successfully completed a £3 million fundraise to cover the expected operating costs for the remainder of the current financial year. We raised this money with a single counterparty in a transaction that was executed overnight as we believed this was the most effective way to secure the working capital needed while protecting value as much as possible.

Given the weakness of the traditional AIM follow on funding market for companies such as ours, our funding strategy going forward is, wherever possible, to raise money from industry and joint venture partners rather than from existing or new equity investors. In Tanzania we are looking for a substantial farm out partner, most likely a multinational helium user, specialist financial institution or much larger industry participant. In Colorado, we look forward to increasing contributions from the wells already on production.

During the year, we welcomed Nishant Dighe to the role of Non-Executive Director. Nishant has an extensive background in engineering and business, holding master’s degrees in both Chemical Engineering and Petroleum Engineering from Imperial College London, as well as an MBA from Warwick Business School. He has over thirty years of experience across a broad range of organisations, including roles at ExxonMobil, strategic consultancy with Marakon Associates, and as COO and interim CEO of Oslo-listed Panoro Energy. Most recently, he served as CEO of RAK Gas, the National Oil and Gas Company of Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, and as CEO of the RAK Petroleum Authority.

In addition, Sarah Cope was appointed as an Executive Director, taking up the role of Head of Governance and Compliance, having previously served as a Non-Executive Director. Sarah’s extensive experience as a Nomad/broker and investment banker will support the wider team as the Company continues to progress its strategy.

James Smith took the decision to step down from his role as Non-Executive Chairman, having joined the Board in 2020 as a Non-Executive Director and served as Non-Executive Chairman since August 2023. On behalf of the Board, I would like to thank James for his guidance and contribution during his tenure.

In April, I was delighted to join the Board as Non-Executive Chairman. I have significant public company experience as a Non-Executive Director and Chairman, having been Chairman of several AIM companies in recent years, with direct experience in, amongst others, the oil and gas, oilfield services and mining sectors. I am currently Chairman of AIM-listed Caspian Sunrise plc and Built Cybernetics plc.

I am also a fellow of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (FCA) and was, for 25 years, a fellow of the Association of Corporate Treasurers (FCT). While working in the UK broking industry, I gained more than 15 years’ experience as a Qualified Executive under the AIM Rules, where I ran the Corporate Finance departments of several of the larger and more active Nominated Adviser firms.
I look forward to working with the team utilising my extensive knowledge of both the capital markets and resources arenas to further deliver our strategy and objectives.

The attractiveness of the helium sector has resulted in a number of new entrants over the past few years, several of whom are making encouraging progress, which we welcome as it is good for the sector and those listed on the London market at a time when other sectors are struggling.

Against this positive macro and thematic backdrop, we continue to assess new opportunities both within and outside of our existing asset portfolio. The Company’s Executive team, led by Lorna Blaisse, are true helium professionals and provide us with the expertise to be entrepreneurial and flexible in our assessment of opportunities as they arise.
We therefore look forward to the future with confidence.

I am pleased to report a year of major milestones for the Group in the twelve months ended 30 June 2026. We delivered tangible progress across our assets in the USA and Tanzania, advancing our ambition to build a helium business that creates long-term value for shareholders. With first helium sales achieved shortly after the year end and a landmark mining licence secured in Tanzania, we enter the next phase of our development with a clear focus on delivery.

Helium supports critical and unsubstitutable applications in semiconductor manufacturing, MRIs, defence, advancement in AI and aerospace, making supply security a strategic priority for high tech end-users. Since March 2026, it is reported that around one-third of the global helium supply has been offline following disruption in the Middle East. Separately, the United States Geological Survey (“USGS”) reports that the US imported 423 mmcf in 2024, with Qatar supplying 28% of US imports over 2021–2024. Today, the US is largely relying on its own domestic production of helium. These figures underline the case for new, geographically diversified global supplies.

At Galactica-Pegasus in Colorado, USA, where the Company holds a 50% interest, we reached a major milestone with the commissioning of the Piñon Canyon processing facility and the tie-in of six development wells drilled in the previous year. First helium sales followed shortly after the reporting period, marking an exciting new chapter for the Company and its shareholders. Our focus now is on scaling up production, progressing further development infill drilling across Galactica and pursuing continued expansion into Pegasus.

In Tanzania, we secured a landmark achievement in July 2025: the award of the 480 km² southern Rukwa Mining Licence (“ML”). This is Tanzania’s first helium mining licence and the largest mining licence ever awarded in the country—an important step towards developing this unique project for production. With an active farm-out campaign underway, we are encouraged by the interest the project is attracting as we seek a long-term partner. Securing that partnership and advancing southern Rukwa towards production are clear priorities as we build on the year’s achievements.

The Galactica-Pegasus Project in Colorado, USA, in which the Company has a 50% interest, achieved first gas from the Piñon Canyon Plant in December 2025. This was followed by rigorous commissioning of the gathering system and production facility ahead of first helium sales in July 2026.

Achieving first gas at Galactica was a major milestone for the Company and our joint venture, marking tangible progress towards establishing a reliable, scalable source of helium for the US market. The subsequent supply constraints arising from the US-Iran conflict have reinforced the importance of supply diversification, as end-users seek alternative sources and greater security of supply. We are focused on building on this achievement as we work towards realising the project’s commercial potential.

The Galactica-Pegasus Project is emerging as an attractive new domestic supply option for US helium and CO₂ buyers seeking to diversify and strengthen their sourcing portfolios. Blue Star Helium (the “Operator”) has been engaging directly with a wide range of potential off-takers, ranging from large-scale transport and bulk storage providers to mid and small-scale transport operators, packaged gas distributors, and key end-use sectors.
During the first half of 2026, the Operator focused on plant and production optimisation, with six wells tied into the Piñon Canyon processing facility by late March.

Planning and permitting have advanced for additional tie-ins and infill drilling designed to increase production from the Piñon Canyon processing plant. In addition, the Operator continues commercial discussions regarding co-producing CO2 and liquefaction. These activities are focused on expanding gas processing capacity and supporting revenue growth through 2026 and into 2027.

In June 2026, the Operator signed an initial 3-month helium purchase and sales agreement covering all helium produced at the Piñon Canyon Plant. This agreement was subsequently extended at the end of August to 31 March 2027, supporting the project’s commercial progress.

This first formal helium offtake commitment was an important commercial milestone for the joint venture. Together with trailer-by-trailer spot sales of initial production, it provided a platform from which to pursue longer-term offtake arrangements.

First helium sales from the Piñon Canyon Plant were achieved in July 2026 at spot prices, followed by the commencement of sales under the short-term offtake agreement at the end of that month. With trailer fills now taking place regularly, the joint venture is building on this significant step in the project’s commercial development.

Looking ahead, the joint venture is focused on building on this progress. The Operator plans to deepen three existing wells at Galactica during Q4 2026. followed by drilling of a further 9 wells in 2027, subject to the necessary permissions being granted.

Southern Rukwa achieved a landmark milestone in July 2025 with the award of its 480km² mining licence (“ML”), Tanzania’s first helium mining licence and the largest mining licence area ever awarded in the country. Songwe Helium Ltd, our joint venture with the Tanzanian Government, was incorporated and its directors appointed, with Helium One holding an 83% interest and the Government a 17% free carried interest.

The Framework Agreement and Shareholders’ Agreement were formally executed at a signing ceremony in the Songwe region on 2 May 2026. I attended alongside Graham Jacobs, our Commercial and Finance Director, Songwe Helium Ltd directors and our senior in-country team, together with local Government officials, representatives from the Ministry of Minerals and Mining Commission, stakeholders and local communities.

At ITW-1, we used our Predator 220 rig to re-enter the well, recover the completion string and production packers, and prepare for Electrical Submersible Pump (“ESP”) operations in January 2026. Testing ran from 26 January to 14 February, with equipment supplied and operated by CenerTech Group, part of CNOOC, running for over 450 hours without maintenance or downtime.

The ESP delivered a sixfold increase in flow rate compared with the 2024 extended well test’s natural flow, reaching up to the equivalent of 16,400 bpd and averaging 15,000 bpd at a maximum pump frequency of 55 Hertz. Helium concentrations remained sustained, averaging 5.4% and peaking at 9.2% (both air corrected), with no decline over time. Rapid wellhead and downhole pressure recovery after shut-in indicated a wider connected resource.

Measured temperatures of 90°C suggested that helium is transported to surface primarily within fluids diluted by the Karoo aquifer; undiluted Basement-derived fluids would be hotter based on the known geothermal gradient at the Itumbula High. We continue to assess fluid sources and interactions and evaluate further drilling and testing targets, likely focused on fractured Basement elsewhere across the ML area.

Building on these encouraging results, we launched a formal farm-out process in May 2026 to secure a suitable industry partner and third-party financing for southern Rukwa’s next phase. PVE Consulting Ltd (“PVE”) is leading the process, bringing more than 20 years’ upstream management-services experience and a track record in transaction support and exploration and production mandates across Africa and other regions.

I am pleased to report that our health and safety performance continued to be exceptional, with no lost time incidents recorded during operations. During the re-entry of ITW-1 and the ESP operations, Helium One’s internal HSE management system recorded a total of three incidents over approximately 19,299 man hours of work (excluding 19,299 hours of time on site on rest periods). These comprised of medical treatment and equipment failure, with zero trauma-related incidents.
FINANCIAL RESULTS FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30 JUNE 2026

The Group recorded a total comprehensive loss attributable to the equity holders of the Company of US$3,413,295, a decrease compared with US$4,857,406 for the year ended 30 June 2025. This decrease is mainly as a result of a far lower share option expense being incurred in the year under review.
The Group’s net assets as at 30 June 2026 were US$67,919,638, compared with US$53,202,847 at 30 June 2025. At 30 June 2026, the Group’s cash position was US$6,552,494 (30 June 2025: US$3,152,755).

The Board determined that in respect of the Galactica-Pegasus project, the project had progressed from the exploration and evaluation phase into the development phase.  Accordingly, the carrying value of the related exploration and evaluation assets of $7,641,287 was reclassified to Development assets (See notes 11 and 12). The reclassification represents a transfer between categories of non-current assets and had no impact on the Group’s profit or loss or total net assets for the year.
More information on this reclassification of assets can be found in the notes to the accounts.

We enter the year ahead with clear priorities and a strong sense of purpose. Having made the transition to helium production and sales at Galactica-Pegasus, our focus is to build on this milestone while securing a partner to fund field development at the southern Rukwa Helium Project and advance it towards production.

Global events, including the US-Iran conflict and the shut-in of Qatar’s Ras Laffan plant in Q1 2026, have highlighted the vulnerability of helium supply chains. The resulting supply constraints have driven up helium prices, with some spot prices reported to have been ca. US$2,000 per mcf, reinforcing the importance of developing reliable, geographically diversified sources of supply.

Against this backdrop, I believe our portfolio offers a compelling opportunity to contribute to future helium supply. We remain focused on progressing our projects and engaging with strategic partners and offtakers, with the aim of translating our operational achievements into sustainable, long-term value for shareholders.

Helium’s essential role in high-technology industries underpins its strategic importance. On 23 October 2026, the US Department of Energy added helium to its critical materials list, recognising the risk of supply disruption and its vital role in semiconductor manufacturing supporting quantum computing, AI infrastructure and data centres. The Board believes our portfolio has the potential to help meet increasing demand for this irreplaceable resource.

On behalf of the Company, I thank our staff, partners and stakeholders for their dedication and contribution throughout the year. I also extend our appreciation to the local communities, landowners and Government stakeholders whose continued co-operation supports our operations. To our shareholders, thank you for your continued support. We look ahead with confidence, committed to delivering on our priorities and keeping you informed as we progress our projects.

The principal activity of Helium One Global Limited (the ‘Company’) and its subsidiaries (together the ‘Group’) is the exploration and development of helium gas resources. The Company is incorporated and domiciled in the British Virgin Islands. The address of its registered office is 171 Main Street, PO Box 92, Road Town, Tortola, VG1110, British Virgin Islands. The Company is exempt from preparing separate parent company Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2026 in line with BVI Business Companies Act 2004.

The Company’s ordinary shares are admitted to trading on the Alternative Investment Market (AIM) of the London Stock Exchange under the ticker ‘HE1’. The Company is also quoted on Börse Frankfurt with symbol 9K3.

The determination of an entity’s functional currency is assessed on an entity-by-entity basis. A company’s functional currency is defined as the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates. The functional currency of the Parent Company is the US Dollar, because it operates in the BVI, where the majority of its transactions are in US dollars. The functional currency of the Tanzanian subsidiaries is Tanzanian Shillings in which currency the subsidiaries incur payroll costs, licence fees, withholding tax fees and payments to local suppliers, and are required to report and file accounts locally. The functional currency of the US Subsidiary is the US Dollar in which currency the subsidiary incurs operational costs.
The functional and presentational currency of the Group for year ended 30 June 2026 is US dollars. The presentational currency is an accounting policy choice.

The principal accounting policies that have been used in the preparation of these consolidated Financial Statements are set out below. These policies have been consistently applied unless otherwise stated.

The consolidated Financial Statements have been prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and IFRS Interpretations Committee (IFRS IC) interpretations as adopted by the European Union applicable to companies under IFRS and in accordance with AIM Rules. The Financial Statements are prepared on the historical cost basis or the fair value basis where the fair valuing of relevant assets or liabilities has been applied.

The preparation of Financial Statements in conformity with IFRS requires management to make judgements, estimates and assumptions that affect the application of policies and reported amounts of assets and liabilities, income and expenses. The estimates and associated assumptions are based on historical experience and factors that are believed to be reasonable under the circumstances, the results of which form the basis of making judgements about carrying values of assets and liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources. Actual results may differ from these estimates.

The estimates and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Changes in accounting estimates may be necessary if there are changes in the circumstances on which the estimate was based, or as a result of new information or more experience. Such changes are recognised in the period in which the estimate is revised.

Subsidiaries are entities controlled by the Group. The Group controls an entity when it is exposed to, or has rights to, variable returns from its involvement with the entity and could affect those returns through its power over the entity. The Financial Statements of subsidiaries are included in the consolidated Financial Statements from the date on which control commences until the date on which control ceases.
The investments in subsidiaries held by the Company are valued at cost less any provision for impairment that is considered to
have occurred, the resultant loss being recognised in the income statement.

The Group accounts for its interests in joint arrangements in accordance with IFRS 11 Joint Arrangements. A joint operation is an arrangement whereby the parties having joint control have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities relating to the arrangement.

Where the Group has an interest in a joint operation, it recognises its share of the assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses arising from the arrangement in the relevant line items of the consolidated financial statements, in accordance with the applicable IFRS Accounting Standards.
Joint control exists where decisions about the relevant activities require the unanimous consent of the parties sharing control.

Non-controlling interests represent the portion of equity in subsidiaries not attributable, directly or indirectly, to the owners of the parent company. Non-controlling interests are recognised separately from the equity attributable to owners of the parent in the consolidated statement of financial position.

Profit or loss and each component of other comprehensive income are attributed to the owners of the parent and to non-controlling interests, even if this results in the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance.

Changes in the Group’s ownership interests in subsidiaries that do not result in a loss of control are accounted for as equity transactions. Any difference between the adjustment to non-controlling interests and the fair value of consideration paid or received is recognised directly in equity attributable to the owners of the parent
The consolidated Financial Statements incorporate the financial statements of the Company and its subsidiaries up to 30 June 2026.

Intra-group balances and transactions, and any unrealised income and expenses (except for foreign currency transaction gains or losses) arising from intra-group transactions, are eliminated. Unrealised losses are eliminated in the same way as unrealised gains, but only to the extent that there is no evidence of impairment.

Transactions in foreign currencies are translated into the respective functional currencies of Group companies at the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions. Monetary assets and liabilities denominated in foreign currencies are translated into the functional currency at the exchange rate at the reporting date. Non-monetary assets and liabilities that are measured at fair value in a foreign currency are translated into the functional currency at the exchange rate when the fair value was determined. Non-monetary items that are measured based on historical cost in a foreign currency are translated at the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Foreign currency differences are recognised in profit or loss and presented on the statement of comprehensive income.

The assets and liabilities of foreign operations and fair value adjustments arising on acquisition, are translated into United States Dollars at the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions. Foreign currency differences are recognised in OCI and accumulated in the translation reserve, except to the extent that the translation difference is allocated to OCI. When a foreign operation is disposed of in its entirety or partially such that control, significant influence or joint control is lost, the cumulative amount in the translation reserve related to that foreign operation is reclassified to profit or loss as part of the gain or loss on disposal.

If the Group disposes of part of its interest in a subsidiary but retains control, then the relevant proportion of the cumulative amount is reattributed to OCI. When the Group disposes of only part of an associate or joint venture while retaining significant influence or joint control, the relevant proportion of the cumulative amount is reclassified to profit or loss.

The consolidated Financial Statements have been prepared on a going concern basis. The Group incurred a net loss of $3,413,295 and incurred operating cash outflows of $114,476 and is not expected to generate positive cash flows from operations in the next 12 months from the date at which these consolidated Financial Statements were approved.

During the year, the Group started to transition the Galactica project from exploration to development-stage with the Rukwa project expected to follow. As a result, operational activity levels and development expenditure are expected to increase significantly relative to prior periods. Management has continued to advance its exploration and development projects and maintain a disciplined approach to the allocation of capital.

On 14 October 2026, the Company announced that it had raised gross proceeds of £3,000,000. The placing is expected to strengthen the Group’s liquidity position and provide additional funding towards its development projects. The extent to which the proceeds extend the Group’s cash runway is dependent on the net funds received, the timing of expenditure and the Group’s ongoing funding requirements.

In preparing the going concern assessment, the Directors reviewed detailed cash flow forecasts covering the going concern assessment period. These forecasts incorporate the Group’s approved work programmes, committed expenditure, contractual obligations, corporate overheads and planned development activities.

The principal judgement applied by the Directors relates to the timing and quantum of future expenditure associated with development activities and the extent to which such expenditure remains within the control of management. The forecasts reflect the current project plan and include assumptions regarding development schedules, procurement timelines, permitting activities and associated costs.
The Directors have considered a range of sensitivities, both individually and collectively, to the base case forecast, including:
•        increases in development and operating costs;
•        adverse movements in foreign exchange rates where applicable;
•        the timing of future financing activities.
The Directors have identified a number of measures available to manage liquidity and preserve cash resources should actual expenditure or project progress differ from current forecasts.

These include the deferral or reprioritisation of discretionary development activities, postponement of non-essential capital expenditure, reductions in corporate and consultancy expenditure, and the pursuit of additional equity funding, project financing or strategic investment arrangements.

The Group continues to evaluate potential farm-in and strategic investment opportunities in relation to the southern Rukwa project, which could reduce future funding requirements. Such arrangements remain subject to negotiation and cannot be assured.
Material uncertainty relating to going concern

The Group’s ability to meet its forecast expenditure is dependent on the successful management of its development programmes, the timing of anticipated project cash flows and, where necessary, access to additional funding.

Although the post-year-end equity placing represents a significant contribution towards the Group’s funding requirements, the Directors recognise that further funding will be required to support the Group’s development activities and operating expenditure during the forecast period. The majority of expected capital expenditure within the forecast period is discretionary rather than committed expenditure and although there is a degree of flexibility on when the expenditures are incurred, the Board do not want to delay unnecessarily the progress of the Company’s projects.

These conditions indicate the existence of a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on the Group’s and Company’s ability to continue as a going concern and, therefore, their ability to realise their assets and discharge their liabilities in the normal course of business.
Notwithstanding this uncertainty, the Directors consider that the Group has reasonable prospects of securing additional funding and implementing appropriate cash preservation measures when required.

Accordingly, the Directors have a reasonable expectation that the Group and Company will have adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future and have therefore prepared these financial statements on a going concern basis. The financial statements do not include any adjustments that would be required if the going concern basis of preparation were inappropriate.

INTANGIBLE ASSETS - EXPLORATION AND EVALUATION ASSETS

The Group applies the full cost method of accounting for Exploration & Evaluation (‘E&E’) costs, having regard to the requirements of IFRS 6 Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral Resources. Under the full cost method of accounting, costs of exploring for and evaluating mineral resources are accumulated by reference to appropriate cost centres being the appropriate licence area and / or licence areas held under licence agreements. A licence agreement grants the right to explore and evaluate mineral resources, and to acquire the licences later at the discretion of the licence holder. Exploration and evaluation assets are tested for impairment as described further below. Where appropriate, licences may be grouped into a cost pool.

All costs associated with E&E are initially capitalised as E&E assets, including payments to acquire the legal right to explore, costs of technical services and studies, seismic acquisition, exploratory drilling, and testing.

Exploration and evaluation costs include directly attributable overheads together with the cost of materials consumed during the exploration and evaluation phases. Costs incurred prior to having obtained the legal right to explore an area are expensed directly to profit and loss as they are incurred.

E&E assets are assessed for impairment when facts and circumstances suggest that the carrying amount may exceed its recoverable amount. Such indicators include, but are not limited to, those situations outlined in paragraph 20 of IFRS 6 Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral resources and include the criteria for which a determination is made as to whether commercial reserves exist.
The aggregate carrying value is compared against the expected recoverable amount, by reference to the present value of future cash flows expected to be derived from production of commercial reserves.
When a licence or pool of licences is abandoned or there is no planned future work, the costs associated with the respective licences are written off in full.
Any impairment loss is recognised in profit and loss and separately disclosed.
The Group considers each licence, or where appropriate pool of licences, separately for purposes of determining whether impairment of E&E assets has occurred.
E&E Costs are not amortised prior to the conclusion of appraisal activities.

E&E costs assets related to each exploration licence or pool of licences are carried forward until the technical feasibility and commercial viability has been demonstrated and that the project has progressed from the exploration and evaluation phase into the development phase.

Once the technical feasibility and commercial viability of extracting a mineral resource is demonstrable, the related E&E assets are assessed for impairment on an individual licence or cost pool basis, as appropriate, as set out below and any impairment loss is recognised in profit and loss. The carrying value, after any impairment loss of the relevant E&E assets is then reclassified as Development Assets within Property, Plant and Equipment.

All capitalised exploration and evaluation assets are monitored for indications of impairment. Where a potential impairment is indicated, assessment is made for the group of assets representing a cash generating unit.
In accordance with IFRS 6 the Group firstly considers the following facts and circumstances in their assessment of whether the Group’s exploration and evaluation assets may be impaired:
(a)              the period for which the Group has the right to explore in the specific area has expired during the period or will expire in the near future, and is not expected to be renewed.
(b)             substantive expenditure on further exploration for and evaluation of resources in the specific area is neither budgeted nor planned.

(c)              exploration for and evaluation of resources in the specific area have not led to the discovery of commercially viable quantities of mineral resources and the Group has decided to discontinue such activities in the specific area.

(d)             sufficient data exist to indicate that, although a development in the specific area is likely to proceed, the carrying amount of the exploration and evaluation asset is unlikely to be recovered in full from successful development or by sale.
In addition to the above, the Group gives due consideration to the following criteria:
•                 unexpected geological occurrences render the resource uneconomic;
•                 a significant fall in realised or estimated prices render the project uneconomic; or
•                 an increase in operating costs occurs.
If any such facts or circumstances are noted, the Group perform an impairment test in accordance with the provisions of IAS 36.

The aggregate carrying value is compared against the expected recoverable amount of the cash generating unit, defined as the smallest identifiable group of assets that generates cash inflows largely independently of the cash inflows from other assets or groups of assets. The recoverable amount is the higher of value in use and the fair value less costs to sell. An impairment loss is reversed if the assets or cash-generating unit’s recoverable amount exceeds its carrying amount. A reversal of impairment loss is recognised in the profit or loss immediately.

A provision is recognised in the Statement of Financial Position when the Group or Company has a present legal or constructive obligation because of a past event, and it is probable that an outflow of economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation. If the effect is material, provisions are determined by discounting the expected future cash flows at a pre–tax rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and, where appropriate, the risks specific to the liability.

Deferred income taxes are calculated using the Statement of Financial Position liability method on temporary differences. Deferred tax is provided on the difference between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities and their tax bases. However, deferred tax is not provided on the initial recognition of goodwill or on the initial recognition of an asset or liability unless the related transaction is a business combination or affects tax or accounting profit. Deferred tax on temporary differences associated with shares in subsidiaries and joint ventures is not provided if reversal of these temporary differences can be controlled by the Company and it is probable that reversal will not occur in the foreseeable future. In addition, tax losses available to be carried forward as well as other income tax credits to the Company are assessed for recognition as deferred tax assets.

Deferred tax liabilities are provided in full, with no discounting. Deferred tax assets are recognised to the extent that it is probable that the underlying deductible temporary differences will be able to be offset against future taxable income. Current and deferred tax assets and liabilities are calculated at tax rates that are expected to apply to their respective period of realisation, provided they are enacted or substantively enacted at the Statement of Financial Position date.

Changes in deferred tax assets or liabilities are recognised as a component of tax expense in the income statement, except where they relate to items that are charged or credited directly to equity, in which case the related current or deferred tax is also charged or credited directly to equity.

The Company awards share options to certain Directors and employees to acquire shares of the Company. Additionally, the Company has issued warrants to providers of equity finance. All goods and services received in exchange for the grant of any share–based payment are measured at their fair values in accordance with IFRS 2. Where employees are rewarded using share–based payments, the fair values of employees’ services are determined indirectly by reference to the fair value of the instrument granted to the employee.

The fair value is appraised at the grant date and excludes the impact of non–market vesting conditions. Fair value is measured by use of the Black Scholes model. The expected life used in the model has been adjusted, based on management’s best estimate, for the effects of non–transferability, exercise restrictions, and behavioural considerations. All equity–settled share–based payments are recognised as an expense in the income statement with a corresponding credit to “other reserves.”

If vesting periods or other non–market vesting conditions apply, the expense is allocated over the vesting period, based on the best available estimate of the number of share options expected to vest. Estimates are subsequently revised if there is any indication that the number of share options expected to vest differs from previous estimates. Any cumulative adjustment prior to vesting is recognised in the current period. No adjustment is made to any expense recognised in prior years if share options exercised are different to that estimated on vesting. Upon exercise of share options, the proceeds received net of attributable transaction costs are credited to share premium. On expiry or cancellation of an option, the attributable transactions costs are debited to the share premium with a corresponding credit to retained earnings.

A gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss when a financial liability is settled through the issuance of the Company’s own equity instruments. The amount of the gain or loss is calculated as the difference between the carrying value of the financial liability extinguished and the fair value of the equity instrument issued. A gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss on the expiry of a financial liability. The amount of the gain or loss is calculated as the difference between the carrying value of the expired financial liability and the fair value of the equity instrument issued.

The Group’s financial assets consist of financial assets held at amortised cost. The classification depends on the purpose for which the financial assets were acquired. Management determines the classification of its financial assets at initial recognition.
Financial assets held at amortised cost

Assets that are held for collection of contractual cash flows, where those cash flows represent solely payments of principal and interest, are measured at amortised cost. Any gain or loss arising on derecognition is recognised directly in the profit or loss and presented in other gain/ (losses) together with foreign exchange gains and losses. Impairment losses are presented as a separate line item in the statement of profit or loss.

They are included in current assets, except for maturities greater than 12 months after the reporting date, which are classified as non-current assets. The Group’s financial assets at amortised cost comprise trade and other current assets and cash and cash equivalents at the year-end.

Regular purchases and sales of financial assets are recognised on the trade date – the date on which the Group commits to purchasing or selling the asset. Financial assets are initially measured at fair value plus transaction costs. Financial assets are de-recognised when the rights to receive cash flows from the assets have expired or have been transferred, and the Group has transferred substantially all of the risks and rewards of ownership.
Financial assets are subsequently carried at amortised cost using the effective interest method.

The Group assesses, on a forward-looking basis, the expected credit losses associated with its financial assets carried at amortised cost. For trade and other receivable due within 12 months the Group applies the simplified approach permitted by IFRS 9. Therefore, the Group does not track changes in credit risk, but rather recognises a loss allowance based on the financial asset’s lifetime expected credit losses at each reporting date.

A financial asset is impaired if there is objective evidence of impairment as a result of one or more events that occurred after the initial recognition of the asset, and that loss event(s) had an impact on the estimated future cash flows of that asset that can be estimated reliably. The Group assesses at the end of each reporting period whether there is objective evidence that a financial asset, or a group of financial assets, is impaired.
The criteria that the Group uses to determine that there is objective evidence of an impairment loss include:
•        Significant financial difficulty of the issuer or obligor;
•        A breach of contract, such as a default or delinquency in interest or principal repayments;
•        The Group, for economic or legal reasons relating the borrower’s financial difficulty, granting the borrower a concession that the lender would not otherwise consider; and
•        It becomes probable that the borrower will enter bankruptcy or other financial reorganisation.
The Group first assesses whether objective evidence of impairment exists.

The amount of the loss is measured as the difference between the asset’s carrying amount and the present value of estimated future cash flow (excluding future credit losses that have not been incurred), discounted at the financial asset’s original effective interest rate. The asset’s carrying amount is reduced and the loss is recognised in profit or loss.

If, in a subsequent period, the amount of the impairment loss decreases and the decrease can be related objectively to an event occurring after the impairment was recognised (such as an improvement in the debtor’s credit rating), the reversal of the previously recognised impairment loss is recognised in profit or loss.

Trade payables are obligations to pay for goods or services that have been acquired in the ordinary course of business from suppliers. Accounts payable are classified as current liabilities if payment is due within one year or less. If not, they are presented as non-currently liabilities.
Trade payables are recognised initially at fair value, and subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method.
Other financial liabilities are initially measured at fair value. They are subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method.
Financial liabilities are de-recognised when the Group’s contractual obligations expire or are discharged or cancelled.

TERMS AND VALUATION OF THE LONG-TERM INCENTIVE AWARDS (LTIP)

The Company operates a discretionary Long-Term Incentive Plan (LTIP) under which share options and conditional share awards may be granted to eligible employees and executive directors. Awards ordinarily vest after three years, subject to continued employment and the satisfaction of any performance conditions determined by the Remuneration Committee. Share options may be exercised following vesting for a period of up to ten years from the grant date.

Awards generally lapse on termination of employment, subject to certain good-leaver provisions. The Remuneration Committee may impose a post-vesting holding period, generally up to two years, and all awards are subject to malus and clawback provisions.

The Plan limits awards to 75% of an employee’s annual base salary and restricts the aggregate allocation of shares under employee share plans to 10% of issued ordinary share capital over a rolling ten-year period. The value of the awards is amortised over the vesting period and expensed accordingly. The Group’s objective when managing capital is to safeguard the entity’s ability to continue as a going concern and develop its mineral exploration and development and other activities to provide returns for shareholders and benefits for other stakeholders.

The Group’s capital structure comprises all the components of equity (all share capital, share premium, retained earnings when earned and other reserves). When considering the future capital requirements of the Group and the potential to fund specific project development via debt, the Directors consider the risk characteristics of the underlying assets in assessing the optimal capital structure.

The Group’s activities expose it to a variety of financial risks: market risk (including foreign currency risk and price risk), credit risk and liquidity risk. The Group’s overall risk management programme focuses on the unpredictability of financial markets and seeks to minimise potential adverse effects on the Group’s financial performance.
The fair values of the Company’s financial instruments on 30 June 2026 and 30 June 2025 did not differ materially from their carrying values.
The Group measures fair values using the following fair value hierarchy that reflects the significance of the inputs used in making the measurements:

•            Level 1 fair value measurements are those derived from inputs other than quoted prices that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly (i.e. as prices) or indirectly (i.e. derived from prices).

•            Level 2 fair value measurements are those derived from valuation techniques that include inputs for the asset or liability that are not based on observable market data (unobservable inputs).

•            Level 3 assets are assets whose fair value cannot be determined by using observable inputs or measures, such as market prices or models. Level 3 assets are typically very illiquid, and fair values can only be calculated using estimates or risk-adjusted value ranges.

Market risk arises from the Group’s use of interest bearing and foreign currency financial instruments. It is the risk that future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in interest rates (interest rate risk), and foreign exchange rates (currency risk). No such instruments are held by the Group and therefore no risk has been identified.
Price risk arises from the exposure to equity securities arising from investments held by the Group. No such investments are held by the Group and therefore no risk has been identified.

The Group operates internationally and is exposed to foreign exchange risk arising from various currency exposures, primarily with respect to the Pound sterling, US Dollar and Tanzanian Shilling. Foreign exchange risk arises from recognised monetary assets and liabilities, where they may be denominated in a currency that is not the Group’s functional currency. While the Tanzanian Shilling has depreciated marginally since 1 July 2025 (from 1 TZS = 0.000379 USD to 1 TZS = 0.000381 USD) the Tanzanian Shilling risk is mitigated by the fact that Helium One would only have one month’s cash requirement on hand at any one time and this is usually held in US Dollars. Another significant risk in Tanzania is a US Dollar risk as the loans to Tanzanian subsidiaries are denominated in US Dollars. The Directors consider that, for the time being, no hedging or other arrangements are necessary to mitigate this risk.

Credit risk is the risk that the Group will suffer a financial loss as a result of another party failing to discharge an obligation and arises from cash and other liquid investments deposited with banks and financial institutions. The Group considers the credit ratings of banks in which it holds funds to reduce exposure to credit risk. The Group will only keep its holdings of cash and cash equivalents with institutions which have a minimum credit rating of ‘BBB’.

Whilst the cash holdings are deposited with institutions in terms of the policy, the Group considers that it is not exposed to any significant increases in credit risk and no Expected Credit Loss has been recognised.
The Group considers that it is not exposed to major concentrations of credit risk.

The Group holds cash as a liquid resource to fund its obligations. The Group’s cash balances are held primarily in US Dollars. The Group’s strategy for managing cash is to assess opportunity for interest income whilst ensuring cash is available to match the profile of the Group’s expenditure. This is achieved by regular monitoring of interest rates and monthly review of expenditure forecasts. Short term interest rates on deposits have for the fiscal year been very unattractive.

The Group has a policy of not hedging and therefore takes market rates in respect of foreign exchange risk; however, it does review its currency exposures on an ad hoc basis. Currency exposures relating to monetary assets held by foreign operations are included within the foreign exchange reserve in the Group Balance Sheet.

In addition to equity funding, additional borrowings have been secured in the past to finance operations.
